keyVerseText: And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.
rootMeaning: The word οὐδέποτε (oudépote) is formed from the combination of οὐδέ, meaning 'neither' or 'not even,' and ποτέ, meaning 'at any time.' This etymology emphasizes a complete negation across all time, conveying the sense of 'never at any time' or 'not even once.' Beyond the simple English gloss 'never,' the root sense highlights an absolute exclusion, stressing that something has not occurred at any point, past, present, or future.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, οὐδέποτε appears 16 times and is most frequently translated as 'never' (8 occurrences), with other renderings including 'at any time' and variations of 'have ye never.' This consistency in translation underscores its function as a strong adverb of negation, often used to deny any occurrence or experience whatsoever. Its use with various tenses, including past, present, and future, reflects its flexibility while maintaining its core meaning of absolute negation.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, οὐδέποτε's meaning of 'never at any time' serves as a powerful reminder of God's perfect knowledge and judgment. It underscores the reality that God’s recognition and relationship with individuals are not conditional or partial but absolute. When Scripture uses this term, it often highlights the finality of divine rejection or the certainty of an experience never having occurred, such as knowing a person. This absolute negation invites believers to examine their standing before God, emphasizing the necessity of genuine faith and obedience to be truly known by Him.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 7:23, the phrase 'I never knew you' employs οὐδέποτε to convey a complete and irrevocable denial of relationship by Jesus toward those who practice iniquity. The word's forceful meaning intensifies the warning that no claim to association with Christ will be accepted if it is not accompanied by righteous living. This use of οὐδέποτε powerfully communicates the finality of being unknown by Christ, urging believers to seek a sincere and enduring connection with Him.
